\title{Can Referees Rely on Automated Reference Checks?\\Diagnosing and Reducing False Alarms in CheckIfExist}

\author{
    Diletta Abbonato\textsuperscript{1,*} \\
    \small \textsuperscript{1}CPS Department, University of Turin, Turin, Italy \\
    \small \textsuperscript{*}Corresponding author: \texttt{diletta.abbonato@unito.it}

\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent Automated reference checks are entering peer review, and referees are increasingly expected to run them. Such a tool helps a referee only if it surfaces the references that are wrong without burying them among references that are correct. An independent evaluation of five tools found that the most sensitive of them flag about half of the genuine references in a manually verified test set. This paper takes one of those tools, CheckIfExist, and asks where its false alarms come from and whether they can be removed without loss of detection. A diagnosis combining the source code with \Nrefs{} reference strings from \Npapers{} arXiv and NeurIPS papers traces the errors to identifiable properties of citation practice, PDF extraction and bibliographic indexing, whose prevalence varies considerably across fields. After revising the tool, we first reproduce the published result on the independent test set and then evaluate the revision on it: the revised tool detects \IndRevTP{} of \IndProb{} problematic references while flagging \IndRevFP{} of \IndGen{} genuine ones, against \IndBaseTP{} and \IndBaseFP{} for the original version and \IndRCTP{} and \IndRCFP{} for RefChecker as reported by the independent study. On a set of \ConAlt{} altered references constructed after the revision was fixed, detection rises from \ConDetBase{}\% to \ConDetRev{}\%, while the share of genuine references flagged moves from \ConFARBase{}\% to \ConFARRev{}\%. On whole manuscripts, the flags a referee must inspect fall from \CorpFlagMeanBase{} to \CorpFlagMeanRev{} per paper. We would maintain that the binding constraint on automated reference checking is not detection but restraint, and that much of what limits restraint lies in the scholarly record rather than in any particular tool.

\vspace{6pt}
\noindent \textbf{Keywords:} Peer review; Reference verification; Citation accuracy; Research integrity; Bibliographic databases; Large language models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Reference verification has moved into the editorial workflow. Language models fabricate bibliographic references under a wide range of conditions \citep{bhattacharyya2023, walters2023, day2023}, and a series of recent audits documents such references in the published record itself, in conference proceedings and on preprint servers alike \citep{sakai2026, zhao2026, russinovich2026}. Publishers now screen submissions, arXiv suspends authors who submit unchecked machine-generated references \citep{naturebanned2026}, and referees are increasingly expected to check the bibliographies of the manuscripts they review. A number of tools have appeared to help them, ranging from open scripts to services combining database retrieval with language models \citep{abbonato2026, russinovich2026, shi2026, khajavi2026}.

What a referee needs from such a tool can be stated simply. It should surface the references that are wrong, and it should not bury them among references that are correct. The two requirements pull in opposite directions, since every rule that makes a checker more suspicious also makes it suspicious of more genuine references, and a referee confronted with many flags per manuscript will reasonably stop reading them. The literature on citation verification has concentrated on the first requirement. Evaluations report how many fabricated references a system detects, typically on benchmarks in which fabrications are generated for the purpose, and it is generally acknowledged that performance on references observed in the wild is lower \citep{shi2026}. The second requirement has received much less attention, and yet it is the one that determines whether a tool is usable in peer review at all.

Independent evidence suggests that it is also the binding one. \citet{badalova2026} compared five verification tools on references from three scholarly documents, each manually checked against publisher and repository records. The tools that detected nearly all problematic references also flagged a large share of genuine ones, and the authors conclude that none was reliable enough to support a decision without manual verification. They attribute the difficulty to reference extraction errors, incomplete metadata, limited database coverage and inconsistent verification results. The present paper takes one of the tools they evaluated, CheckIfExist, of which the author is the developer \citep{abbonato2026}, and asks three questions. Where do its false alarms come from? Can they be removed without loss of detection? And what, as a result, does a referee see when checking a whole manuscript?

The answers are sought in three steps. The first is a diagnosis that combines a reading of the source code with a large corpus of reference strings extracted from the bibliographies of preprints and conference papers, audited for this study. The second is a revision of the tool addressing each cause identified, fixed before evaluation. The third is an evaluation on the independent test set of \citet{badalova2026}, where the published result is first reproduced, on a set of altered references constructed after the revision was fixed, and on whole manuscripts. The comparison with RefChecker \citep{russinovich2026}, which the same independent study evaluated, provides an external benchmark.

The exercise is of interest beyond the tool. The causes identified turn out to be properties of citation practice and of the bibliographic infrastructure rather than of the software: the division of DOI registration between agencies that are queried separately, citation styles that omit titles and are concentrated in particular fields, the text layer of compiled PDFs, and the incompleteness of author lists in open metadata. They will therefore affect every checker built on the same open sources, and any bibliometric study that relies on such checks to estimate the prevalence of fabricated or erroneous citations.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{sec:data} describes the tool, its revision and the evaluation design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports where the errors come from, how the revised tool performs, and what a referee sees. Section~\ref{sec:disc} discusses the implications and the limitations of the evidence.

\section{Data and methods}
\label{sec:data}

\subsection{The instrument and its revision}
\label{sec:tool}

CheckIfExist is an open-source web application, running entirely in the browser, that verifies bibliographic references against five open sources: Crossref, OpenAlex \citep{priem2022}, Semantic Scholar, arXiv and DBLP \citep{abbonato2026}. It is deterministic, in the sense that it uses no language model and applies explicit rules to the records it retrieves, and only reference strings leave the user's machine, never the manuscript itself. A reference can be checked individually, as part of a pasted bibliography, from a BibTeX file, or from a PDF whose bibliography the tool extracts. In each case the result is shown with one of four labels: \emph{Verified} when the match confidence exceeds 80, \emph{Partial Match} above 50, \emph{Mismatch} below, and \emph{Not Found} when no source returns a sufficiently similar record. We treat any label other than Verified as a flag, that is, as a reference the referee must inspect, which is also the definition used by \citet{badalova2026}.

The revision addressed each cause of error identified in the diagnosis of Section~\ref{sec:diagnosis}, and Table~\ref{tab:revision} lists them. The causes fall into two groups. The first concerns references that were accepted when they should not have been, and the corresponding checks can only lower the confidence of a match, never raise it. The second concerns genuine references that were flagged, and here the revisions either find the record by other means or report the reason a reference cannot be checked, instead of reporting it as not found.

The revision was fixed in the public repository before any evaluation began. Two further corrections were made later and are reported as such. One, found while evaluating on the independent test set, prevents the year check from reading a year out of an arXiv identifier. The other, found while measuring the prevalence of title-less references in the diagnostic corpus, makes the detection of title text independent of letter case, so that a title cited in title case is not mistaken for a missing one. Both were made before the constructed set and the manuscripts were evaluated with the revised tool.

\subsection{Evaluation design}
\label{sec:design}

Four sets of references are used, for different purposes. The \emph{diagnostic corpus} consists of \Nrefs{} reference strings extracted from the bibliographies of \Npapers{} arXiv preprints and NeurIPS proceedings papers spanning 2016 to 2026, in nine venue-year strata, and serves to measure how often the features associated with errors occur. It was audited for this study: every string left unresolved by a single-source check, and a stratified random sample of the strings it accepted, were resolved individually, and the identifier or URL supporting each verdict is released with the data.

The \emph{independent test set} is that of \citet{badalova2026data}: \IndN{} references from \IndDocs{} documents, of which \IndProb{} were judged problematic by manual verification and \IndGen{} genuine, released with the outputs of the five tools. The public file was saved in an encoding that cannot represent typographic quotes, dashes or some Central European letters, and \IndRestoredChars{} characters in \IndRestoredRefs{} references had been replaced by question marks. They were restored by rules that follow from the citation styles of the three documents, and every substitution is logged.

The \emph{constructed set} was built after the revision was fixed, from \ConGen{} references of the diagnostic corpus whose Crossref record matched on title and year, re-fetched by DOI and formatted in APA style. Each yields a genuine reference and an altered one, \ConKindN{} of each of four kinds: an \emph{invented} work, keeping the first author but splicing the title with that of another reference from the same stratum; an \emph{extended} title, in which a real title is followed by invented words; \emph{swapped} authors, in which a real title carries the authors of another paper; and \emph{altered} metadata, in which title and authors are correct but year and venue are not. The first three are fabrications, the fourth a citation error of the kind a referee should still notice. Half of the pairs carry the real DOI in both versions, since fabricated references often carry real identifiers.

The \emph{manuscripts} are \CorpMss{} whole bibliographies from the diagnostic corpus, three per stratum, comprising \CorpRefs{} reference strings as extracted from the PDFs, and serve to measure what a referee would see per paper.

The tool was run outside the browser on the same code path as the web interface, with three differences that do not touch its logic. A standard XML parser replaces the browser's; requests that the tool routes to arXiv through a public proxy, needed in the browser for cross-origin reasons, go to arXiv directly; and requests are paced at the rates the sources ask for, with retries on transient errors except to Semantic Scholar, which the tool itself does not retry. Every response, failures included, was stored, so that the original and the revised tool saw identical responses to identical requests and differences between them measure the tool rather than the network. Semantic Scholar's unauthenticated service was frequently unavailable, answering \STwoAnswered{}\% of the \STwoRequests{} requests made to it during the evaluation; this is also the condition of a browser user without a key, and it affects the original and the revised tool alike.

RefChecker \citep{russinovich2026} provides the external comparison. On the independent set we use the results published by \citet{badalova2026}, obtained in its default configuration. On the constructed set we ran version 3.0.190 ourselves, without a language model. In that configuration it cannot segment a plain-text bibliography, so both tools were given the same BibTeX file, which CheckIfExist processes through its own BibTeX path.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Where the errors come from}
\label{sec:diagnosis}

The audit of the diagnostic corpus provides the starting point. A single-source check of the kind commonly deployed, submitting each string to Crossref and accepting the first record returned, leaves \Nflag{} strings unresolved, and individual resolution found no fabricated reference among them: the flags consisted of segmentation failures, text that is not a reference, references the rule could not match, and works no source indexes. The same check is, if anything, more worrying in the other direction, since only \Pcmatchcorrect{}\% of the references it accepts correspond to the work cited and \Pcmatchwrong{}\% resolve to a different publication. A permissive check thus produces false alarms and false reassurance at once, and a referee has no way of telling which is which.

The source code of CheckIfExist shows how the same two failures arise in a tool that queries several sources and compares what it retrieves. The misses have a common origin in acceptance rules that ask whether a record is compatible with the citation rather than whether it is the work cited: containment of a title, trust in an identifier, and a year disagreement that was computed and then discarded. The false alarms have more varied origins, and most of them are properties of the references and of the indexes rather than of the software. Table~\ref{tab:features} reports how often the corresponding features occur in the diagnostic corpus.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Features of reference strings associated with errors of automated checking, as a percentage of strings in each stratum of the diagnostic corpus. Title-less references are single references with no stretch of four or more words between punctuation marks; merged entries contain several references run together.}
\label{tab:features}
\vspace{4pt}
\input{table_features}
\end{table}

Three patterns stand out. The first is the dependence on field. References that carry no title, the norm in the styles of physics and astronomy, are \FeatNoTitleGen{}\% of the strings in the general 2026 cohort, where those fields are represented, against \FeatNoTitleNipsTwentythree{}\% in NeurIPS 2023; a checker that matches on titles fails on them systematically, and fails more often in some fields than in others. The second is the dependence on time, which runs in both directions. Ligature glyphs in the extracted text, which the original normalization deleted, occur in \FeatLigCsSixteen{}\% of the arXiv \textit{cs.AI} strings of 2016 and in almost none of 2026, while arXiv identifiers, which route verification through a path that did not compare authors, grow from \FeatArxivCsSixteen{}\% to \FeatArxivCsTwentyfive{}\% of \textit{cs.AI} references between 2016 and 2025. The third is the weight of extraction itself. Entries that are not references at all reach \FeatNotRefNipsTwentyfive{}\% of the NeurIPS 2025 strings, and merged entries are most frequent, at \FeatMergedGen{}\%, in the cohort that includes astronomy bibliographies, whose unnumbered styles give a PDF segmenter nothing to split on.

\label{sec:performance}

Table~\ref{tab:independent} reports the results on the independent test set. The first step is replication. Run through the single-reference path, which appears to be the one the independent study used, the original tool reproduces the published confusion matrix within two cases in each cell, with row-level agreement of \IndAgreeQuick{}\%; through the pasted-bibliography path the agreement is \IndAgreePaste{}\%. The residual differences are consistent with the fluctuating availability of sources at different times, and they concern genuine references rather than problematic ones.

The revised tool detects \IndRevTP{} of the \IndProb{} problematic references, against \IndBaseTP{} for the original, and flags \IndRevFP{} of the \IndGen{} genuine ones, against \IndBaseFP{}: false alarms fall by \IndFPDrop{}\% while detection does not decline. Figure~\ref{fig:independent} places the two versions of CheckIfExist among the five tools evaluated by the independent study. Before the revision all of them, CheckIfExist included, lie along a frontier on which greater detection is bought with more false alarms; the revised tool moves off that frontier rather than along it.

\subsection{What a referee sees}
\label{sec:referee}

The unit a referee works with is the manuscript, not the reference, and the relevant question is how many references must be inspected per paper and what they consist of. \pending{per-manuscript results: text to be written from the completed runs}

\section{Discussion and conclusions}
\label{sec:disc}

This paper has asked whether a referee can rely on an automated reference check, taking one open tool as the object of study. The evidence suggests that the answer depends less on the tool's ability to find problematic references, which was already high, than on its ability to leave correct references alone, and that the second can be improved substantially once the causes of false alarms are identified. On the independent test set the revision reduces false alarms by \IndFPDrop{}\% without loss of detection. \pending{one sentence on the constructed set and one on manuscripts, from the completed runs}

For referees, the practical implication concerns how a flag should be read. A flag from a verification tool is not a finding but an instruction to look, and its value lies in how much looking it saves. The revised tool distinguishes flags that call for scrutiny of the citation, such as a title that extends the record's, authors the record does not list, or a year that disagrees, from flags that describe the limits of the check, such as an extraction problem or a web page that no bibliographic database indexes. The second kind still requires a glance, but not suspicion. It seems likely that the credibility of automated checking in peer review will depend on this distinction as much as on the aggregate rates.

For those building such tools, three lessons seem to generalise. The first is that acceptance rules should test identity rather than compatibility: a record whose title is contained in the citation, or whose identifier appears in it, is compatible with the citation without being the work cited, and the most common fabrications exploit precisely that gap. The second is that a resolved identifier is not evidence that a citation is correct, only that it points somewhere; the remainder of the citation has to agree with where it points. The third is that open bibliographic infrastructure is heterogeneous in ways that a checker must represent explicitly. DOIs are registered by more than one agency, author lists in open metadata are sometimes incomplete, some citation styles omit the title altogether, and free interfaces are rate limited to the point of intermittent unavailability. None of these is a defect of any single source, and none is visible in an evaluation that uses fabrications alone.

For bibliometric research, the results add to a well-documented literature on database coverage \citep{martinmartin2018, visser2021, verabaceta2019} a point specific to the verification of references. The error rates of a checker depend on the citation styles and extraction conditions of the literature it is applied to, and those vary across fields and over time, as Table~\ref{tab:features} shows. Estimates of the prevalence of fabricated citations that rely on automated checks, and comparisons of such estimates across fields or periods, therefore inherit a bias whose direction and size depend on the checker's rules. It would seem prudent for such studies to report the false-alarm behaviour of their checker on genuine references from the same fields, alongside its detection rate.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The independent test set is small and was assembled as a convenience sample, and a few of its cases were inspected during the diagnosis, so that it cannot be treated as fully held out. The constructed set was built after the revision was fixed, but its alterations are generated by rule, following the typology of fabrications reported in the literature \citep{russinovich2026, shi2026}, and fabrications produced by language models in the wild may differ from them. The corpus covers computer science, quantitative biology and one general cohort, in texts almost entirely in English, and the prevalence of the features in Table~\ref{tab:features} will differ elsewhere. The evaluation ran the tool outside the browser, with differences that do not touch its logic but do affect which sources were available when, and Semantic Scholar was frequently unavailable throughout. The author developed the tool she evaluates; the use of an independently built and labelled test set, the reproduction of its published result, and the release of all code, data and responses are intended to limit, not remove, the consequences of that position. Finally, no referee was observed using the tool. Whether the reduction in false alarms translates into time saved and errors caught in actual peer review is an empirical question that a study with referees would need to address, and it is the natural next step.

The conclusion we would draw is a cautious one. Automated reference checking can already detect most problematic references, and on the evidence reported here it can also be made considerably more restrained. What limits it is, to a large extent, not the software but the scholarly record it consults: the way references are extracted, the styles in which they are written, and the coverage and completeness of the open metadata against which they are checked. A referee can rely on such a tool to direct attention, and not to replace it.

\section*{Use of AI tools}
\pending{draft below, to be checked and confirmed by the author before submission}
During this study the author used an AI coding assistant (Claude, Anthropic) to write and run the evaluation harness and the analysis code, to implement the revisions to the CheckIfExist source code described in Section~\ref{sec:tool}, and to draft and edit parts of the manuscript. The individual resolution of references in the audit of the diagnostic corpus was also carried out by the assistant, with programmatic access to bibliographic sources and to web search, and each verdict is recorded against a named identifier or URL in the released data; no inter-rater reliability statistic is therefore available for that audit. The author reviewed the code, the revisions, the audit records and the text, and takes full responsibility for the content of the paper.
